title: Joshua 8:18–29
context: Joshua 8:18–29 narrates the capture and destruction of Ai. At the LORD’s command, Joshua stretches out his javelin toward the city, the ambush rises and sets it on fire, and the men of Ai are caught between the two Israelite forces. The inhabitants are put to death, the king is captured, and the city is burned and left as a heap. Israel keeps only the livestock and goods, as the LORD had permitted. The king’s body is hanged until evening and then taken down, in line with Deuteronomy 21:22–23. The language of total destruction belongs to the herem commands of Deuteronomy 7 and 20, given for the conquest of the land, and interpreters differ on how literally its sweeping language should be read. Both traditions read it within that unique covenant and historical setting, not as a pattern for later warfare or for the church.

verses.text: The LORD said to Joshua, “Stretch out the javelin that is in your hand toward Ai, for I will give it into your hand.” Joshua stretched out the javelin that was in his hand toward the city.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Joshua, “Stretch out the javelin that is in your hand toward Ai, for I will give it into your hand.” Arminian readers note that the gesture is a signal of obedience and faith. Joshua acts on God’s word, and his action becomes the sign that God is fulfilling his promise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD again speaks first and the victory is credited to him: “I will give it into your hand.” Joshua’s raised javelin recalls Moses’ raised hand in Israel’s early battles, marking the outcome as God’s work. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing God’s initiative and Joshua’s obedient response working together.

verses.text: The ambush arose quickly out of their place, and they ran as soon as he had stretched out his hand and entered into the city and took it. They hurried and set the city on fire.
verses.arminianNotes: The ambush rises “quickly” and takes the city “as soon as he had stretched out his hand,” then sets it on fire. Arminian readers note the readiness of the ambush, which had waited patiently and acted immediately when the signal came, an example of faithful obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the precise timing as confirming that the operation followed God’s direction. The burning of the city carries out the command of 8:8. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the fulfillment of God’s plan and as showing the value of prompt obedience.

verses.text: When the men of Ai looked behind them, they saw, and behold, the smoke of the city ascended up to heaven, and they had no power to flee this way or that way. The people who fled to the wilderness turned back on the pursuers.
verses.arminianNotes: The men of Ai see “the smoke of the city ascended up to heaven,” and they have “no power to flee this way or that way.” Arminian readers note the sudden reversal: the pursuers become the trapped, and the Israelites who fled toward the wilderness turn back on them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image of smoke rising to heaven as marking the city’s judgment in the sight of God. The enemy is left powerless because God has given them into Israel’s hand. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the decisive turning point of the battle, the clear reversal of Israel’s defeat in chapter 7.

verses.text: When Joshua and all Israel saw that the ambush had taken the city, and that the smoke of the city ascended, then they turned back and killed the men of Ai.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua and all Israel see that the ambush has taken the city, and they turn back and kill the men of Ai. Arminian readers note that the whole people act together in this victory, just as the whole people suffered the consequences of sin in chapter 7. Corporate responsibility runs both ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the coordinated action of the two forces fulfills the plan given in 8:4–8. God’s promise is realized through Israel’s united obedience. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly as part of a war narrative in Israel’s unique setting, without treating its violence as a general model.

verses.text: The others came out of the city against them, so they were in the middle of Israel, some on this side, and some on that side. They struck them, so that they let none of them remain or escape.
verses.arminianNotes: The forces from the city come out, and the men of Ai are caught “in the middle of Israel,” with none allowed to “remain or escape.” Arminian readers acknowledge the grim totality of the account and read it within the herem commands of the conquest (Deuteronomy 20:16–17), which were specific to that time and place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse within the herem commands, noting that Deuteronomy 20:18 gives their stated purpose: “that they not teach you to follow all their abominations.” Shared ground: both traditions take the text seriously as God’s judgment in a unique moment of redemptive history, and both note that interpreters differ on how literally the sweeping language should be read.

verses.text: They captured the king of Ai alive, and brought him to Joshua.
verses.arminianNotes: The king of Ai is captured alive and brought to Joshua. Arminian readers note that the king’s fate is held over for judgment, which the narrative will describe in 8:29, and that his capture shows the completeness of Israel’s victory over the city’s leadership.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the capture of the king fulfills the LORD’s promise in 8:1, “I have given into your hand the king of Ai.” God’s word is fulfilled precisely. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a simple narrative fulfillment of God’s promise and as preparation for the closing scene of the battle.

verses.text: When Israel had finished killing all the inhabitants of Ai in the field, in the wilderness in which they pursued them, and they had all fallen by the edge of the sword until they were consumed, all Israel returned to Ai and struck it with the edge of the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel finishes killing the inhabitants of Ai in the field and then returns to strike the city. Arminian readers acknowledge the difficulty of such passages and read them within the conquest’s covenant setting, where Scripture presents judgment on the Canaanites as falling after long patience (compare Genesis 15:16, “the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full”).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the conquest as an act of divine judgment on the wickedness of the nations, as Deuteronomy 9:5 says: “for the wickedness of these nations the LORD your God does drive them out.” Shared ground: both traditions refuse to treat the text as a model for later warfare, and both read it in light of Scripture’s whole testimony to God’s justice and mercy.

verses.text: All that fell that day, both of men and women, were twelve thousand, even all the people of Ai.
verses.arminianNotes: Twelve thousand fall that day, “both of men and women,” described as “all the people of Ai.” Arminian readers acknowledge the human weight of this number and read it with sober clarity. The text records it as judgment within the herem command, and it is not softened, nor is it presented as a pattern for God’s people today.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse soberly, as part of God’s judgment carried out through Israel in a unique redemptive-historical moment. They note that the same judgment fell on Achan within Israel, showing that God’s holiness was not partial. Shared ground: both traditions recognize that interpreters differ on the reading of such numbers and language, and both refuse speculation beyond the text.

verses.text: For Joshua didn’t draw back his hand, with which he stretched out the javelin, until he had utterly destroyed all the inhabitants of Ai.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua does not draw back his hand with the javelin “until he had utterly destroyed all the inhabitants of Ai.” Arminian readers note Joshua’s steadfast obedience to the full command, in contrast to Achan’s partial and secret disobedience. Faithfulness is complete, not selective.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the raised javelin, like Moses’ raised hands, signals that the victory belongs to God and is carried through to the end he commanded. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as emphasizing complete obedience to God’s word in the setting of herem, while recognizing the gravity of what that obedience involved.

verses.text: Israel took for themselves only the livestock and the goods of that city, according to the LORD’s word which he commanded Joshua.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel takes “only the livestock and the goods,” “according to the LORD’s word which he commanded Joshua.” Arminian readers note the contrast with Achan: this time Israel receives plunder lawfully, by God’s permission, rather than seizing it in disobedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD’s word governs even the plunder: what is taken is taken by his command. His people receive good things from his hand rather than grasping them. Shared ground: both traditions see the verse as a quiet commentary on chapter 7, showing that obedience brings blessing that disobedience tried to steal.

verses.text: So Joshua burned Ai and made it a heap forever, even a desolation, to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua burns Ai and makes it “a heap forever, even a desolation, to this day.” Arminian readers note the lasting memorial of judgment, which serves as a warning to future generations of the seriousness of opposing God’s purposes. Set beside the heap over Achan in 7:26, it reminds readers that the same holy God judged sin both inside and outside Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the narrative’s repeated phrase “to this day,” linking the event to later readers and inviting them to remember God’s acts. The heap stands as a sign of God’s judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a memorial, and both note that the text makes a theological rather than an archaeological claim about the site.

verses.text: He hanged the king of Ai on a tree until the evening. At sundown, Joshua commanded, and they took his body down from the tree and threw it at the entrance of the gate of the city, and raised a great heap of stones on it that remains to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: The king of Ai is hanged on a tree “until the evening,” and at sundown his body is taken down and covered with a heap of stones. Arminian readers note that Joshua follows the law in Deuteronomy 21:23, “his body shall not remain all night on the tree.” Even in war, Israel is bound by God’s law.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the hanging on a tree the background of Deuteronomy 21:23, “he who is hanged is accursed of God,” which Paul applies to Christ: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Galatians 3:13). Shared ground: both traditions note the parallel heaps of stones over Achan (7:26) and the king of Ai, marking judgment within and outside Israel alike.
